copies.headline: Noah's Backfield Can't Cover John's Tight Ends
copies.body:
The margin lives at tight end and the third receiver. John gets Brock Bowers (16) and Trey McBride (14) — two starting-caliber options where Noah has Colston Loveland (12) and Brenton Strange (8). McBride's Cardinals are 10.5-point road dogs at the Chargers with a 46.5 total, which is the exact script that turns a tight end into a target hog. Puka Nacua at 21 is questionable but plays in the week's biggest game, Rams-Niners at 48.5, and Matthew Stafford throws in it too. That's a stacked correlation Noah can't answer.
Noah's edge is the backfield, De'Von Achane (18) and James Cook III (15) for a seven-point cushion, but Achane's game is a 40.5-point plod in Vegas with Miami getting points. Mike Evans and Josh Downs both carry tags, and behind them it's Michael Wilson at 10. John's #11 power ranking is a preseason artifact; this roster is deeper than it reads.

copies.headline: Isaac's Injury Report Is Longer Than His Bench
copies.body:
Isaac's whole case is the receiver room, and it comes with five question marks. Ja'Marr Chase in a 50.5-total game against Tampa is the single best asset on either roster, and Malik Nabers gets a 48.5 total with the Giants catching points, which usually means late volume. But if Chase and Nabers both sit, the WR3 slot falls to Adonai Mitchell and the +5 edge evaporates instantly. Behind Bo Nix in Kansas City — a 42.5 total, the lowest number on the board for either team — sits Malik Willis. That is not a backup plan, that is a hostage situation.
Kaleb wins the other three spots and does it with cleaner games. Justin Herbert as a 10.5-point favorite with Ladd McConkey, plus Drake London chasing in Pittsburgh, plus Harold Fannin at tight end where Isaac has two nine-point guys. Jeanty and Hall carry tags too, but RJ Harvey exists and Isaac's ceiling is entirely contingent on inactive lists. Twelfth-ranked roster, thinnest margin for error.

copies.headline: CJ's Receiver Room Is A Waiting Room
copies.body:
Grant wins this at wide receiver or not at all. Amon-Ra St. Brown gets New Orleans in a 49.5-total game Detroit is favored to control, and even with Zay Flowers questionable, Grant can slide Jaylen Waddle or Christian Watson in without much bleeding — 45 from his top three against CJ's 39. CJ's problem is that his best three includes Emeka Egbuka with a tag and Parker Washington, and if Egbuka sits he's starting Alec Pierce as a WR2 in a game Indianapolis is getting 3.5 in. That's a real hole, not a rounding error.
Running back is dead even on paper, but CJ's depth chart is a hospital ward — Pacheco on IR, Charbonnet out, Hubbard and Henderson both questionable — so Jonathan Taylor and Quinshon Judkins carry it alone. Joe Burrow in a 50.5 shootout with Tampa is the one clean CJ edge, worth two points over Kyler Murray. Not enough to cover the receiver gap.

copies.headline: Logan's Eagles Stack Outguns Adam's Depth
copies.body:
The math is simple and it isn't kind to Adam: Logan is up four at quarterback with Jalen Hurts and five at running back with Saquon Barkley, and both of those points come from the same game Adam's Jayden Daniels is stuck chasing in. Philadelphia laying 5.5 with a 44.5 total is the profile where the favorite grinds, Barkley eats fourth-quarter carries and Hurts vultures at the goal line. Daniels will throw plenty and probably run for a score, but 17 against a stacked 39 is a hole. Adam's counterpunch is receiver, where Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Chris Olave in a 49.5-total game in Detroit and Rome Odunze give him a two-point edge, plus Sam LaPorta or Mark Andrews at tight end.
That's four points of surplus against nine of deficit, and Adam's questionable tags sit on the wrong guys. Logan's injury notes barely matter with Xavier Worthy and Rashid Shaheed behind them; Adam's tight end room is a coin flip between two banged-up names. Kenneth Walker in a 42.5-total Kansas City game is the thin backfield floor Logan doesn't have. Power ranking says Adam is the better team over sixteen weeks. This week, the roster read says otherwise.

copies.headline: Peter's Depth Is A Rumor, Not A Roster
copies.body:
The top lines are nearly identical — 31 to 31 at running back, 44 to 42 across three receivers, Lamar Jackson buying Peter two points over Trevor Lawrence in a Ravens-Colts game with a 48.5 total. So this comes down to who survives Sunday morning. Christian has Chase Brown and Travis Etienne locked into a 40.5-total Jaguars grinder and a 49.5 Saints shootout where New Orleans is chasing seven points and throwing to Etienne late. CeeDee Lamb and DeVonta Smith are both playing in games their teams are favored to control. Kittle's questionable, but Chig Okonkwo is a real fallback.
Peter's problem is everything behind Bijan Robinson and George Pickens. Tucker Kraft is his only tight end and he's tagged. Tee Higgins is questionable in the week's best game (50.5 total), and Jalen Nailor at 8 is what replaces him. Brooks and Monangai are both dinged. That's five question marks on a roster with no answers underneath them.

copies.headline: Leif's Backfield Outweighs Mitchell's Lunchbox
copies.body:
The margin lives at running back, where Leif can start Derrick Henry against a Colts team getting 3.5 in a 48.5-total game and David Montgomery as a fallback if Christian McCaffrey's questionable tag turns ugly. Mitchell has Jahmyr Gibbs, who is the single best player in this game with Detroit favored by seven, and then a cliff: Rachaad White is questionable, Josh Jacobs is day-to-day, Kaleb Johnson projects for a point. One bad Sunday inactive report and Mitchell is starting Chris Brooks.
Receiver is Mitchell's actual edge — Nico Collins, Courtland Sutton and DJ Moore beat Leif's top three by three, and Tyler Warren adds a couple at tight end. But that assumes Warren plays. Josh Allen in a 44.5 game against Houston is a steadier floor than Jaxson Dart chasing Dallas, even if Dart's game script is the more entertaining one. Leif's depth wins a close one.

intro: Christian at Peter is the one worth watching all afternoon — two rosters built the same way, running back depth over receiver ceiling, and neither side has a starter with a real injury designation, which means it comes down to whichever backfield the coaching staff decides to split three ways. Leif at Mitchell is the opposite kind of game: Leif fields a top-end quarterback and two receivers attached to offenses favored by a touchdown or more, while Mitchell is leaning on a tight end room and a defense that has to travel. Kaleb, Grant, John and Logan are all favored in games that look like they'll be decided by Sunday night, which is a polite way of saying the Monday game probably won't matter to anyone.
